summary: This informational memo describes practices for accessing the same IMAP4 mailbox from multiple clients, reflecting existing servers and mailing list consensus. It does not define IMAP4 compliance.

plainLanguage.summary: What to do when two people use the same mailbox at once.

questions: what happens when an imap mailbox is deleted while in use
what is an imap expunge response
why should imap clients send noop
subtitle: What IMAP4 servers may do, and what clients must expect, when several clients use one mailbox at once.

tldr.problem: IMAP4 lets servers behave differently in some situations, such as when one client deletes or expunges something other clients are using, so a client written against one server can break on another.
tldr.mechanism: The memo documents the strategies existing servers use for DELETE, RENAME, EXPUNGE, FETCH, STORE, SEARCH and COPY on a multi-accessed mailbox, and tells clients how to cope, mostly by issuing NOOP to receive pending EXPUNGE responses.
tldr.outcome: It helps clients and servers interoperate, but it does not define IMAP4 compliance and is not an exhaustive list of valid behavior.

today: RFC 2180 is an Informational memo and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes practice around RFC 2060, which it relies on for IMAP4 itself.

sections.title: Why Server Behavior Varies
sections.content:
IMAP4 (RFC 2060) is a rich client/server protocol, and within its framework different results are possible for the same interaction. If the protocol did not allow this it would often be unduly restrictive. For example, when several clients use a mailbox and one tries to delete it, the server may choose its solution based on its architecture or preference.

With that flexibility comes greater client responsibility: a client must be written to the behavior the protocol allows, not to one particular server. The memo reflects the practice of some existing servers, or behavior the IMAP mailing list consensus judged reasonable. It is believed to be RFC 2060 compliant, but it does not define IMAP4 compliance.

A multi-accessed mailbox is one that multiple clients access simultaneously. A client has accessed a mailbox after a successful SELECT or EXAMINE.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules let each server do things a little differently, so apps have to be ready for any of the allowed ways.

sections.title: Deleting or Renaming a Shared Mailbox
sections.content:
The memo lists four server strategies. A server MAY:

  • Fail the DELETE or RENAME with a NO. This can be impractical when many clients use a shared mailbox, since there may never be a moment with no one accessing it.
  • Allow DELETE but keep a ghosted mailbox available to clients that already have it, until the reference count of clients reaches 0. New clients cannot see it in LIST or LSUB, and the name cannot be recycled until then. The drawback is that offensive or sensitive content stays reachable.
  • Allow DELETE or RENAME and disconnect the other clients with an untagged BYE. Servers may do this for DELETE but be friendlier for RENAME.
  • Allow RENAME by simply changing the name. Other clients can keep using commands such as FETCH that do not name the mailbox, and find out when they next use the old name. A server MAY add a [NEWNAME] response code to the tagged NO as a hint.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone throws away a box other people are using, the server can say no, let current users finish, kick everyone out, or just change the label on the box.

sections.title: Expunged Messages and Stale Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
The core difficulty is that a client may be in the middle of a command that uses message sequence numbers when another client expunges messages. An EXPUNGE response cannot be sent while responding to a FETCH, STORE or SEARCH, so the client cannot be told immediately. The memo's running scenario has 7 messages, with messages 4:7 marked for deletion and expunged by client 1.

For FETCH, a server MAY keep ghosted copies until it can notify each client, or return responses only for non-expunged messages plus a tagged NO, or return NIL FETCH responses (empty data) for expunged messages and a tagged OK, or fail the EXPUNGE altogether. After a tagged NO, the client SHOULD issue NOOP to collect pending EXPUNGE responses. If a client cannot tell NIL data from an expunged message, it SHOULD also issue a NOOP.

The practical rule for clients is simple: when something looks wrong with sequence numbers, send NOOP to learn what was expunged, then retry.
sections.plainLanguage: If a page is torn out while you are reading it, you cannot be told mid-sentence. So you ask the librarian what changed and then carry on.

sections.title: STORE, SEARCH and COPY
sections.content:
For STORE with the .SILENT suffix, if it succeeds for all non-expunged messages the server SHOULD return a tagged OK. Without .SILENT, if only expunged messages are referenced the server SHOULD return only a tagged NO. For a mix, the server MAY set the flags on the live messages and return a tagged NO, or MAY return a NO and set nothing. In both cases the client SHOULD then issue NOOP and, where needed, reissue the STORE for the surviving messages.

For SEARCH, a server MAY simply leave out expunged messages it has not been able to report. If an expected message is missing, the client SHOULD issue NOOP.

COPY is the only sequence number command that is safe to allow an EXPUNGE response on, because a client may not cascade several COPY commands. The server MAY refuse the copy, or MAY allow it. Either way pending EXPUNGE responses MUST be returned. If a copy fails, the server MUST restore the destination mailbox to its prior state.
sections.plainLanguage: When you try to mark or copy items that may already be gone, the server may do the ones it can and tell you about the rest. Then you check what is missing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The behavior described has the same security considerations as RFC 2060. The memo points out one in particular: some of the behavior does not allow immediate deletion of information when several clients have a mailbox open. That matters for sensitive information where immediate deletion would be preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping a deleted item around for people still looking at it means a secret might not vanish right away.
